, in a population of HIV-infected patients treated with a regimen containing RGV and efavirenz (EFV) (a drug with a low CNS penetration score), we observed a higher rate of neurocognitive disorder in the RGV arm.

, in a small group of patients, RGV was not associated with a significant improvement in neurocognitive disorders and it was not able to penetrate the CNS, as suggested by the lack of correlation between cerebrospinal RGV concentrations and plasma levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CNS is a potential reservoir of HIV, where viral replication may occur in the absence of antiretrovirus, and that antiretrovials should penetrate the CNS as much as possible.
RGV is not expected to have a high penetration into the CNS.

, despite a low lipophilicity, RGV could be able to cross the blood-brain barrier, as shown by a significant increase of its concentration in the cerebrospinalfluid of patients receiving RGV-containing regimens.
